content: Primary dysmenorrhoea is the most prevalent type of menstrual pain, affecting up to 75% of women at some point during their reproductive years. It is characterized by cramping pain in the lower abdomen that begins within the first 8 to 72 hours of menstruation and occurs in the absence of any identifiable organic cause. This review evaluates the evidence for the use of acupuncture (the insertion of needles at specific points on the body) and acupressure (the application of pressure to specific points on the body) as treatments for primary dysmenorrhoea. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture and acupressure in managing primary dysmenorrhoea, comparing these interventions to placebo, no treatment, or conventional medical therapies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared acupuncture or acupressure with sham acupuncture, placebo, usual care, pharmacological treatments, or no treatment. Eligible participants were women of reproductive age experiencing primary dysmenorrhoea during most menstrual cycles or for at least three consecutive cycles, with moderate to severe symptoms. The interventions studied included acupuncture, electro-acupuncture, and acupressure. The primary outcome was pain reduction, while secondary outcomes included menstrual symptoms, quality of life, and adverse effects. A total of 42 RCTs involving 4640 women were included in the analysis. The studies compared acupuncture or acupressure with sham/placebo, medication, no treatment, or other interventions. Many of the continuous data were not suitable for statistical pooling due to evidence of skewness. Acupuncture Studies: 1. Acupuncture versus Sham or Placebo Control (6 RCTs): The findings were inconsistent and inconclusive. The only study with a low risk of bias across all domains found no significant difference between acupuncture and sham/placebo groups at 3, 6, or 12 months. The overall quality of the evidence was low, and no adverse events were reported. 2. Acupuncture versus NSAIDs (Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs): Seven studies reported pain scores using a visual analogue scale (VAS), but the data could not be pooled due to extreme heterogeneity (I² = 94%). In all studies, pain scores were lower in the acupuncture group, with mean differences ranging from 0.64 to 4 points on a 0-10 VAS scale. The evidence was of low quality. Four RCTs reported rates of pain relief, showing a benefit for the acupuncture group (OR 4.99, 95% CI 2.82 to 8.82, 352 women, I² = 0%, low-quality evidence). Adverse events were less frequent in the acupuncture group (OR 0.10, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.44, 4 RCTs, 239 women, I² = 15%, low-quality evidence). 3. Acupuncture versus No Treatment: Data were unsuitable for statistical analysis, but all six studies reporting this outcome found lower pain scores in the acupuncture group. The quality of the evidence was low, and no adverse events were reported. Acupressure Studies: 1. Acupressure versus Sham or Placebo Control: Data were unsuitable for pooling, but two studies reported a mean benefit of 1 to 3 points on a 0-10 VAS pain scale. Four additional studies reported data unsuitable for analysis, all of which found lower pain scores in the acupressure group. No adverse events were reported. The quality of the evidence was low. 2. Acupressure versus NSAIDs: One study assessed this comparison using a 0-3 pain scale. The acupressure group had higher pain scores (indicating more pain) compared to the NSAID group (MD 0.39 points, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.57, 136 women, very low-quality evidence). 3. Acupressure versus No Treatment: There was no clear evidence of a difference between the groups on a 0-10 VAS pain scale (MD -0.96 points, 95% CI -2.54 to 0.62, 2 trials, 140 women, I² = 83%, very low-quality evidence). Authors' Conclusions: The evidence is insufficient to determine whether acupuncture or acupressure is effective in treating primary dysmenorrhoea. For most comparisons, data on adverse events were not available. The quality of the evidence was consistently low or very low, primarily due to risks of bias, poor reporting, inconsistency, and potential publication bias.
